extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in public opinion, political communication, journalism, and policy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how information circulation, social structure, media practices, and individual attention shape the content and quality of public opinion. Useful for studying political communication, media effects, and civic information environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits upon circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: There are very distinct limits upon the circulation of ideas; a large body of fact never reaches the whole public at all, or only very slowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encompasses both active barriers like censorship and privacy interception and the many passive limits (distribution, attention) that prevent facts from reaching everyone. Evaluate informational reach by considering both active suppression and structural limitations on distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effort required to reach ‘everybody’
rubrics_metrics.description: Reaching a nationwide uniform public opinion requires massive, organized effort (e.g., wartime propaganda machinery producing thousands of releases, speeches, posters, lectures, and using many organizations and channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging attempts to form broad public opinion, account for resources, coordination, personnel, and the multiplicity of channels required; absence of such mobilization implies much weaker reach in peacetime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and technical channels shape information supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel and trade, the mails, the wires, radio, railroads, highways, ships, motor cars, and (later) aeroplanes affect the circulation of ideas and the quality of information in intricate ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how transportation and communication infrastructure (and changes to it) enable or constrain flow of information; infrastructural changes can expand or restrict exposure to ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly and scarcity as barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolizing of cables, ports, fuel stations, mountain passes, canals, straits, river courses, terminals, and marketplaces creates barriers upon the exchange of news and opinion. Cost and limited supply can be even greater barriers than monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree of concentration and the cost/availability of distribution channels; consider both legal monopolies and effective scarcity from high costs or limited capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic resources determine access
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a man's income affects his access to the world beyond his neighborhood; with money one can travel, buy books and periodicals, and bring within attention almost any known fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure access inequalities by socioeconomic status; assess how financial means alter the ability to acquire diverse information and thereby influence opinion formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-imposed intellectual limits (curiosity and habits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people are not blocked by external barriers but by lack of appetite and curiosity; they spend spare time on narrow interests and 'cannot really be said to suffer from censorship' but from 'anemia' of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing informational exposure, consider individual preferences, habits, and cultural patterns that limit engagement with broader affairs even when material access exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social set determines admissible sources and judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Each social set decides which authorities and sources of information are admissible; within the social set opinions converge, are sorted, accepted, rejected, judged and sanctioned according to its canons (Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Taste, Form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how group membership influences what information is considered legitimate; social norms and gatekeepers within sets strongly condition uptake and acceptance of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social leaders as custodians and interpreters
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain figures (social leaders, custodians) are recognized as interpreters of a set's pattern and have disproportionate influence in deciding status and acceptable views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify opinion leaders and examine how their endorsements or rejections shape perceptions and act as filters or amplifiers for information across sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal channels vs. mass channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Some individuals have personal channels between sets (people who move in and out) that create direct transmission; for large sections there are no such channels and they must rely on mediated accounts (e.g., novels, moving pictures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate the effects of interpersonal networks versus mass media on transmission and fidelity of information; presence of bridging actors can markedly change circulation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and hierarchical diffusion (‘radiant points’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain social sets act as 'radiant points of conventionality'—the socially superior are imitated by inferiors; imitation extends internationally among elite social sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural and social prestige hierarchies and their role in diffusing norms and opinions; gauge how imitation from elites shapes broader public standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited time and attention devoted to public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: People devote a small amount of time daily to informing themselves about public affairs (empirical estimates suggest many spend about a quarter of an hour on newspapers), so attention is scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for time budgets and attention constraints when evaluating how much information individuals actually process; limited exposure restricts depth and scope of opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of interest across news categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Different audiences prioritize different features (local news, politics, finance, foreign news, editorials). Newspaper space allocation historically reflected these priorities (e.g., large share to news vs. opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare what audiences say they want to how media allocate space; mismatches or shifts in content allocation will affect what parts of public affairs become salient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers and principal media shape data of opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers (with magazines, forums, churches, meetings, films) are the principal means reporting the unseen environment; even when total time is small, these media supply most raw material for opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the dominant media channels in a context and their editorial choices, because they preferentially supply the cues that publics use to form opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and coding reduce informational fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Telegraphy and press-service coding compress and sometimes mutilate original statements (examples of coded dispatches); brief items must 'telescop[e]' complex events and leave out essential elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging accuracy or influence of messages, consider transmission constraints (brevity, coding) that force selective summarization and may distort meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and multiple-stage reporting cause loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Items often pass from eyewitness to commission to correspondent to editor to reader, with translation and selection at each stage; the resulting short accounts cannot carry the full burden of original meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace chains of transmission and examine how each stage (translation, selection) can introduce omissions, bias, or altered emphasis; longer chains increase the likelihood of loss or distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words are imperfect vehicles of meaning; cultural variation in word-value
rubrics_metrics.description: Words do not perfectly map to ideas; the same word evokes different images across readers and national traditions (e.g., 'etonnant' or 'awful'); there is 'war fluctuation on word exchanges' akin to currency exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for semantic variability and cross-cultural differences when evaluating how messages will be interpreted; beware of assuming uniform meanings across audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity of mind as capacity to distinguish and discriminate
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences, and appreciate variety (lucidity) is crucial for sound opinion; differences in lucidity are extensive across individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience sophistication and cognitive skills when judging likely quality of public opinion; training, expertise, and experience increase discriminatory power and depth of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion construction via imagination under sparse messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Because messages are few and situations are complex, most public opinion must be constructed in the imagination from sparse cues; words serve as cues to entire trains of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the role of stereotypes, heuristics, and imaginative filling-in when sparse information is provided; consider how framing and evocative language shape these constructions.
